issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies imply a current external danger/assault-style threat context (arming oneself, hypervigilant scanning for physical threat) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is usually medical and not mitigated by carrying a weapon or scanning for attackers.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Within the profile, these threat-focused safety behaviours are not supported by any Threat items and fit poorly with the formulation, which has Triggers and Threat fully inactive; they suggest a strong trigger/threat loop that the rest of the self-report does not reflect.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness. It is more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral injury and lacks support from the other selected items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding medical cues is plausible for a child's severe illness, but the additional strategies of avoiding public transport and constantly scanning for external threat suggest a danger-based trauma context not represented in the memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: For trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, avoiding public transport is hard to link clinically unless other items indicate transport-related reminders or hospital-travel cues; no such trigger or memory content is present here, so this strategy appears context-mismatched.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Constantly scanning the environment for threat implies an ongoing external danger focus, but the rest of the profile is dominated by trauma-memory disorganisation and self-change appraisals rather than current external-threat concerns. With Threat and Trigger links inactive, this item sits awkwardly in the formulation.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type (child's life-threatening illness) and the rest of the profile. The selected appraisals and memory items center on traumatic recollection, permanent change, and distrust, but not on a current external danger context. 'Constantly scan environment for signs of threat' implies hypervigilance for immediate environmental threat, which is more characteristic of assault/combat-type trauma and is not clinically linked here given that all Triggers and Threat edges are inactive in the formulation. It also sits poorly with the other maladaptive strategies, which are illness/trauma-processing related (avoid care, suppress thoughts).

vignette: Mr. Tran, a 69-year-old widowed man of South Eastern Asian descent, has been a dedicated nanny to his grandchildren since his wife passed away five years ago. His life took an unexpected and tragic turn when one of his beloved grandsons fell severely ill with a life-threatening condition that nearly claimed the child’s life. The memory of that time is seared into Mr. Tran's mind; it feels more real than any ordinary experience he has had. He struggles to articulate what happened even to himself, but the vividness of the event haunts him daily. The memories do not feel like they belong in the past—they feel as though they are happening right now, each moment replaying in his mind with stark clarity. Mr. Tran’s interpretation of this experience has led him to distrust others deeply. He feels that people are not what they seem, and he is certain that the trauma has permanently changed him for the worse. This belief that he has become an unrecognizable person has driven him to avoid medical care or psychological help. Seeking such assistance only serves as a painful reminder of his perceived failures during that critical time. He tries hard not to think about what happened, but when memories inevitably intrude, they feel overwhelmingly present and real, making it difficult for him to distinguish between the past and the present. This difficulty has led Mr. Tran to keep himself occupied all the time, distracting himself with any activity that might temporarily alleviate the overwhelming presence of these memories. His occupation as a nanny has become a double-edged sword. While he finds solace in caring for his grandchildren, it also serves as a constant reminder of the child who nearly died. He fears that by not being vigilant enough or by seeking help, something similar could happen again. This fear exacerbates his avoidance behaviors and distracts him from fully engaging with those around him. Mr. Tran’s struggle has taken a toll on his relationships, particularly with his family members who have noticed his increasing isolation and reluctance to discuss the past. His attempts at mental distraction have led to periods of exhaustion, further deepening his sense of disconnection and self-doubt. The cycle is tightening; as he avoids seeking medical or psychological help, the vividness of his memories increases, reinforcing his negative appraisals about himself and others. He feels trapped in a world where the trauma continues to define him, and each attempt at distraction only serves to highlight the very thing he fears most—his unrecognizable self. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was a recent health scare of his own that forced him to confront the fact that avoiding medical care could have dire consequences. He is most afraid of feeling perpetually trapped by the trauma, but he also hopes for a chance to reclaim a sense of normalcy and connection with those around him.
